clue.text: Led away, was talking incoherently in US dormitory?

definitions.note: a dormitory town, as in American slang for a suburb

indicators.note: sending something away takes it out, so the word Led leaves the longer word

parts.note: to burble is to babble without making sense
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone, led off by the arm, was babbling in a sleepy American commuter town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Led away' reads as being escorted off, but it tells you to remove LED from the end of BURBLED.
explanation.definitionFit: BURB is American slang for a suburb, and a dormitory town is a residential suburb whose people commute out.

clue.text: Two thirds of pail was hot for old bleaching process

indicators.note: taking two thirds of a word keeps four of its six letters and drops the rest

parts.note: a pail is a bucket
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Part of a pail of water was hot, as needed for an old-fashioned way of whitening cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckwash was a former method of bleaching linen by steeping it in hot lye, so the term names an obsolete process.

clue.text: Old stone rubbish receptacle in foreign street

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the receptacle goes within the street

parts.note: rue is French for street
a bin holds rubbish

explanation.surface: An old stone found inside a dustbin on a street abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubine is an archaic word for a ruby, a red precious stone.

clue.text: Spotted playing blinder

indicators.note: playing about with letters moves them around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone was noticed having a brilliant game; a blinder is a superb performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as 'seen', but here it is the definition meaning marked with patches.
explanation.definitionFit: Brindle describes a coat streaked or flecked with darker patches, so a brindle animal is spotted.

clue.text: Ace bolts, galloping — one of several in a race maybe

definitions.text: one of several in a race maybe

indicators.note: galloping suggests wild motion, so the letters are jostled into another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A top horse races off at a gallop, heading for a fence in a steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle race, or a steeplechase, has a series of barriers or hurdles that runners must clear.

clue.text: Duck under blow in wrestling tournament

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part written under another follows it in the answer

parts.note: a bash is a heavy blow
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A wrestler ducks under a punch during a bout.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'wrestling tournament', with 'in' linking it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A basho is one of the official sumo tournaments held in Japan, so it is a competition for wrestlers.

clue.text: Struggled uncommonly as tenor in reworking of Verdi's

indicators.note: placed in something means set inside it, so the tenor goes within the rest
reworking something remakes it, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written, including the s
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: A tenor fought his way through a new production of a Verdi opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncommonly' belongs to the definition: STRIVED is a rarer past tense than strove.
explanation.definitionFit: To strive is to struggle or make great effort, and STRIVED is the less usual past form.

clue.text: Deerhound? Not crazy about matted fur, unkempt

indicators.note: unkempt means untidy and dishevelled, so these letters are tousled out of order
not having something means it is subtracted from the rest of the letters

parts.note: taken as written
crazy is mad

explanation.surface: A dog lover is not worried about a hound's tangled, scruffy coat.
explanation.walkthrough: A subtractive anagram: the letters of MAD come out of 'matted fur' and the remaining six are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tufter is a hound used in stag hunting to drive the deer out of cover, hence a deerhound in a punning sense.

clue.text: Lowly freeman, boss of company hands?

parts.note: a CEO is the chief executive officer who runs a company
the two hands are right and left, R and L

explanation.surface: A humble worker asks whether he is the boss or one of the company's hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceorl was a free man of the lowest rank in Anglo-Saxon England, the origin of churl.

clue.text: Letter for letter

parts.note: surface reading: swapping one letter of the alphabet for another
setter's reading: a Latin adverb for copying exactly, character by character

explanation.walkthrough: This is the Azed competition word, given by definition alone; competitors write their own clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adverb describes a transcription that reproduces a text exactly, keeping every character in place.

clue.text: Decommissioned amphibian navy left out of contingency

indicators.note: something left out of a word is omitted from it

parts.note: in the event of a contingency
N is the abbreviation for navy

explanation.surface: An amphibious vessel is retired, with the navy excluded from planning for emergencies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decommissioned' sounds naval but marks the word as obsolete: EVET is an old form of eft.
explanation.definitionFit: An evet is an archaic name for a newt, an amphibian, and decommissioned signals a word no longer in service.

clue.text: Encroachment for poet, usually with ecstasy switching internal couple

indicators.note: switching a pair swaps their places, here two letters inside the word

parts.note: usu. is the dictionary abbreviation for usually
rapture is ecstatic delight

explanation.surface: A poet usually writes in ecstasy, swapping a couple of lovers round.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second and third letters of the ecstasy word change places.
explanation.definitionFit: Usurpature is a poetic word for usurpation, the wrongful seizing or encroaching on another's rights.

clue.text: Measures, once artist has knocked back his last two

indicators.note: knocking back the final pair turns those two letters round

parts.note: a Cubist is an artist such as Picasso or Braque

explanation.surface: An artist sizes things up the old way after downing his last two drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking, but it turns round the final two letters of the artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, so cubits are measures used in former times.

clue.text: Officer briefly interrupting enemy wave as of old

indicators.note: something interrupting another breaks into it and sits in the middle

parts.note: a foe is an enemy
Lt is the short form of lieutenant

explanation.surface: An officer breaks into the enemy's advancing wave.
explanation.walkthrough: The two officer letters interrupt the enemy separately, one breaking in after its first letter and one after its second.
explanation.definitionFit: Flote is an obsolete word for a wave, hence the clue's marker that it belongs to old usage.

clue.text: Wind formerly cut choice at sea

parts.note: lib is an obsolete verb meaning to geld or castrate

indicators.note: something at sea is lost and confused, so these letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The wind once cut short a decent choice of route while sailing.
explanation.definitionFit: The libecchio is the south-west wind of the Mediterranean, especially around Corsica.

clue.text: Lassie's mink maybe got with a wee bittie allowance

parts.note: a whit is the smallest bit
tret is an old allowance made to buyers for waste in goods

explanation.surface: A Scottish girl obtains her mink coat with only a small allowance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lassie' signals a Scots word, as does 'wee bittie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whittret is Scots for a weasel, and the mink belongs to the same weasel family.

clue.text: Bring round cages i.e. in Germany for kestrel

indicators.note: a phrase that cages something holds it shut within itself

parts.note: to win over someone is to bring them round to your view
d.h., das heisst, is the German equivalent of i.e.

explanation.surface: A falconer persuades a German bird-keeper to lend a kestrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Windhover is a dialect name for the kestrel, from its habit of hovering into the wind, as in Hopkins's poem.

clue.text: Tabby cat, legs going in rear mostly

definitions.note: an old unmarried woman, playfully pictured as a spiteful one

indicators.note: going in means entering, so these letters sit inside the rest
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the stern is the rear of a ship
pins is informal for legs

explanation.surface: A tabby cat tucks its legs in at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat looks like a pet, but tabby is an old word for an elderly unmarried woman, and cat for a spiteful one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabby was once slang for an old maid, the dated sense of an unmarried woman past the usual age to wed.

clue.text: Devil getting end away going after American Honeysuckle?

indicators.note: losing its end means the final letter is removed
one part going after another follows it in sequence

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
Belial is a name for the Devil

explanation.surface: The Devil runs off with an American sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honeysuckle' looks like an endearment, but it is a plant family; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Abelia is a flowering shrub in the honeysuckle family, Caprifoliaceae, so it is an example of that group.

clue.text: Life at university? Pinnacle includes a degree, English

indicators.note: a word that includes others holds them inside it

parts.note: the acme is the highest point
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for degree
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A student's high point at college includes earning a degree in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Academe is the academic world, the environment and community of university life.

clue.text: Sauce coming in a river? The opposite — single lump perhaps

indicators.note: coming in means entering, and 'the opposite' swaps which part holds which

parts.note: HP is a well-known British brown sauce
ea is a dialect word for a river or stream

explanation.surface: Sauce poured into a river forms a single lump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The opposite' reverses the instruction: the river goes into the sauce, not the sauce into the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A heap is a mass of things piled together, which may form a single lump.

clue.text: Linnaean library? Find right book, going into 'Cures'

indicators.note: letters going into a word are placed inside it

parts.note: to cure is to heal
R is the abbreviation for right
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: In a botanist's library, find the right book on remedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbals are books describing plants and their uses, the kind of collection Linnaeus the botanist might own.

clue.text: Gal leaving the country to make a little money abroad

indicators.note: something leaving a word departs from it and is removed

parts.note: Senegal is a country in West Africa
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl emigrates to earn a bit of money overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: The sene is a coin of Samoa, a hundredth of a tala, so a small unit of foreign currency.

clue.text: African bird concealed in old hedge upside down

indicators.note: something in another word sits within it
in a down entry, turning upside down reads the letters from bottom to top

parts.note: haw is an archaic word for a hedge or enclosure
hid is the past tense of hide

explanation.surface: An African bird has been hiding in an overturned old hedgerow.
explanation.definitionFit: The whidah, or whydah, is an African weaver bird with long tail feathers.

clue.text: Opera pieces, often? Not drinking in proper one

indicators.note: one part in the others means placed inside them

parts.note: due means fitting or proper
TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Arias in opera often feature someone sober in a proper scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Duetti is the Italian plural of duetto, a duet, and operas often contain such pieces for two voices.

clue.text: Bully for you, making tons of gold!

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tons
auric means relating to gold, from Latin aurum

explanation.surface: 'Bully for you!' is a congratulation on making a fortune in gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' is not a tormentor or a cheer here; it is the adjective meaning like a bull.
explanation.definitionFit: Tauric means of or like a bull, from Latin taurus, so bully in its literal bovine sense.

clue.text: Weight reduced, one is going in here?

definitions.text: Weight reduced, one is going in here?

indicators.note: going in means entering, so these words sit inside the shortened word

parts.note: wt is the shortened form of weight
a means one
taken as written

explanation.surface: After losing weight, this is the part of you that goes in.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: when you slim down, your middle is where you go in.
explanation.definitionFit: The waist is the narrow middle of the body, the first place a dieter notices getting slimmer.

clue.text: Protection for horse in battle, farm trained, in linked metal

indicators.note: placed in another word means set inside it

parts.note: a chain is a series of linked metal rings

indicators.note: something trained has been reshaped, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warhorse trained on the farm is protected by chainmail.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamfrain, or chamfron, is the armour plate that protected a warhorse's head in medieval combat.

clue.text: Cheeky nonsense, hiding key

indicators.note: hiding something takes it out of sight, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: malarkey is nonsense or humbug
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky bit of nonsense where someone hides the key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' reads as impudent, but it means of the cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Malar is an anatomical adjective meaning relating to the cheek or cheekbone.

clue.text: Family of seafish dried out, in case after treatment

indicators.note: something in another word is placed inside it
something that has been treated has been processed and changed, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
arid means completely dried out

explanation.surface: Seafish dried and packed in a case after being cured.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaridae is the zoological family of parrotfishes, which live in the sea.

clue.text: Il Trovatore, to wit singular opera?

parts.note: sc., scilicet, is Latin for to wit or namely
opera is the plural of opus, so the singular is op., its abbreviation

explanation.surface: Is Il Trovatore, namely, a one-off among operas?
explanation.walkthrough: Il Trovatore is Verdi's opera, but the title translates as the troubadour.
explanation.definitionFit: A scop was an Old English poet or minstrel, the equivalent of a troubadour, which is what trovatore means.

clue.text: Who's ticked off about a bit of lying?

definitions.text: Who's ticked off about a bit of lying?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: chid is an old past tense of chide, to scold

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just a small part of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of lying

explanation.surface: Which person gets told off for telling a little fib?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a youngster scolded for a small lie.
explanation.definitionFit: A child is the typical person reprimanded for a fib, so the question describes a youngster.

clue.text: What pupil did, getting merit in Latin tense

indicators.note: something in two letters sits between them

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Latin
to merit something is to earn it
T is the abbreviation for tense in grammar

explanation.surface: A schoolchild earned a good mark in a Latin tenses test.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil's job is to acquire knowledge, so the past tense of that study verb says what they did.

clue.text: Make sail neat (not half) in a storm, being skilled in such matters

indicators.note: a storm throws everything about, so these letters are tossed into a new order
not half means half of the word is dropped, keeping its first two letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before halving

explanation.surface: A sailor sets sail tidily during a storm, showing real competence at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such matters' points back to the nautical surface, so the definition borrows the clue's own scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamanlike means showing the competence of a good sailor, skilled at handling a ship.

clue.text: It may interest diggers to hold back the rabble

indicators.note: back means the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to hold up or halt is to stop
the herd is the common mass of people

explanation.surface: Something that intrigues gardeners might keep the crowd back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold back' looks like one phrase meaning restrain, but only 'back' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A potsherd is a broken fragment of pottery, of great interest to archaeologists on a dig.

clue.text: Prospect for Scots assured — English missed out twice

indicators.note: missing something out twice means removing two occurrences of it

parts.note: secure means safe or assured
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Scotland's future is guaranteed, with the English left out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Scur is a Scots form of scour, to range over or search an area, as a prospector does.
